title: The Raven
description: A student reading late on a December night to forget the dead Lenore lets in a raven that can say one word, and asks it the questions that will hurt him most.

cover.alt: The raven perched on a bust of Pallas above the chamber door, light fanning out behind
cover.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: Midnight dreary
elements.text: Near midnight in December a scholar dozes over old books, trying to read away his grief for Lenore. Something taps at his chamber door.

metadata.source_quote: Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary,

image.alt: A man asleep over his books at a lamp-lit desk at midnight
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: Sorrow for the lost Lenore
elements.text: The dying embers, the rustling curtains and the memory of Lenore fill him with terrors; he repeats to himself that it is only a visitor.

metadata.source_quote: From my books surcease of sorrow—sorrow for the lost Lenore—

image.alt: A dim room in December: a woman's ghostly figure stands while the man sits by the dying fire
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: Darkness there
elements.text: He apologises to whoever is knocking and throws the door open. There is only darkness. He whispers "Lenore?" and an echo whispers it back.

metadata.source_quote: And the only word there spoken was the whispered word, “Lenore?”

image.alt: The man flinging the door wide open on a dark, empty landing
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: Something at the lattice
elements.text: The tapping comes again, louder, from the window. He tells himself it is the wind.

metadata.source_quote: “Surely,” said I, “surely that is something at my window lattice;

image.alt: The shadow of a raven on an ivy-covered wall beside a shuttered window
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: A stately Raven
elements.text: He opens the shutter and a raven steps in without a bow and perches on the bust of Pallas above his door.

metadata.source_quote: In there stepped a stately Raven of the saintly days of yore.

image.alt: The man throws open the shutter and the raven flies into the room
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: Quoth the Raven
elements.text: Amused, he asks the bird its name. It answers "Nevermore". He decides it learned the word from some unhappy master.

image.alt: The raven perched on a bust of Pallas above the chamber door, light fanning out behind
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: Fancy unto fancy
elements.text: He wheels a cushioned seat in front of the bird and sets about working out what it means, until he remembers that Lenore will never sit on this velvet again.

metadata.source_quote: Then, upon the velvet sinking, I betook myself to linking

image.alt: The man sunk in a velvet chair, lost in thought, a dark hound at his feet
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: Nepenthe
elements.text: The air thickens as if angels swung a censer. He begs to be allowed to forget Lenore.

metadata.source_quote: Quaff, oh quaff this kind nepenthe and forget this lost Lenore!

image.alt: Seraphim swinging a censer around the seated man while the raven watches from the bust
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: Balm in Gilead
elements.text: Calling it prophet and devil, he asks whether there is any cure for his grief, then whether he will meet Lenore in heaven. Nevermore.

metadata.source_quote: Is there—is there balm in Gilead?—tell me—tell me, I implore!

image.alt: The man reaching up toward the raven on the bust, pleading, as smoke rises
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: Bird or fiend
elements.text: He shrieks at the raven to leave and take its beak out of his heart.

metadata.source_quote: “Be that our sign of parting, bird or fiend!” I shrieked, upstarting—

image.alt: The man stands up shrieking at the raven in a shaft of light
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: Still is sitting
elements.text: The raven never leaves. It sits on the bust, its shadow on the floor, and the speaker's soul lies in that shadow for good.

metadata.source_quote: And the Raven, never flitting, still is sitting, still is sitting

image.alt: The man lying on the floor in the raven's shadow, the bird still on the bust above the door
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: The narrator
elements.text: A lonely student who reads to forget the woman he lost. Reasonable at first, he questions the bird into a sentence of despair.

image.alt: The man sunk in a velvet chair, lost in thought, a dark hound at his feet
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: The Raven
elements.text: A black bird "of the saintly days of yore" that knows one word and never moves from the bust of Pallas. Poe called it emblematic of mournful and never-ending remembrance.

metadata.source_quote: Ghastly grim and ancient Raven wandering from the Nightly shore—

image.alt: The raven perched on a bust of Pallas above the chamber door, light fanning out behind
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: Lenore
elements.text: The dead woman the narrator loved. She never appears; she exists only as a name whispered into the dark.

metadata.source_quote: For the rare and radiant maiden whom the angels name Lenore—

image.alt: Angels carrying a maiden through the clouds above a dark sea
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: The chamber
elements.text: A study at night: old books, a lamp, a dying fire, purple curtains and a velvet chair. The whole poem happens inside it.

image.alt: A man asleep over his books at a lamp-lit desk at midnight
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: The chamber door and the bust of Pallas
elements.text: Above the door stands a bust of Pallas Athena, goddess of wisdom. The bird of ill omen settles on wisdom's head.

metadata.source_quote: Perched upon a bust of Pallas just above my chamber door—

image.alt: The raven perched on a bust of Pallas above the chamber door, light fanning out behind
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: The Night's Plutonian shore
elements.text: The darkness the raven seems to come from: Pluto's realm, the shore of the dead.

metadata.source_quote: Tell me what thy lordly name is on the Night’s Plutonian shore!

image.alt: A graveyard by night under a low moon, crosses and tombstones, a raven flying overhead
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: One word
elements.text: The poem's single rule: the Raven can only say "Nevermore". All the meaning comes from the questions.

image.alt: The raven perched on a bust of Pallas above the chamber door, light fanning out behind
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: December night
elements.text: Bleak December, midnight, a storm outside: Poe's setting for maximum melancholy.

image.alt: A dim room in December: a woman's ghostly figure stands while the man sits by the dying fire
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: Answers supplied by the asker
elements.text: The bird's word is random; the man shapes each question so that "Nevermore" will hurt most. Meaning is something the listener brings.

metadata.source_quote: Doubtless,” said I, “what it utters is its only stock and store,

image.alt: The man reaching up toward the raven on the bust, pleading, as smoke rises
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: Grief that wants to be told
elements.text: He does not ask for comfort but for a verdict, and he goes to the one source that can only give the verdict he fears.

image.alt: Two figures walking in a luminous garden among trees, a vision of paradise
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: Remembrance without end
elements.text: The final stanza turns an evening into a permanent state: the raven still sits, the soul is never lifted.

image.alt: The man lying on the floor in the raven's shadow, the bird still on the bust above the door
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: Wisdom crowned by omen
elements.text: The Raven perches on Pallas, goddess of wisdom: reason itself has become the seat of the bird of despair.

image.alt: The raven perched on a bust of Pallas above the chamber door, light fanning out behind
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: Balm in Gilead
elements.text: From Jeremiah 8:22, "Is there no balm in Gilead?": a question about whether any healing is left.

image.alt: The man reaching up toward the raven on the bust, pleading, as smoke rises
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: Nepenthe
elements.text: In the Odyssey, Helen gives Telemachus and Menelaus nepenthe, a drug of forgetfulness for grief.

image.alt: Seraphim swinging a censer around the seated man while the raven watches from the bust
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: Aidenn
elements.text: Poe's spelling of Eden, used for the far-off paradise where he hopes to meet Lenore.

image.alt: Two figures walking in a luminous garden among trees, a vision of paradise
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.

elements.title: Pallas Athena
elements.text: Greek goddess of wisdom; her bust was a common ornament in libraries and studies.

image.alt: The raven perched on a bust of Pallas above the chamber door, light fanning out behind
image.credit: Gustave Doré, engraving for The Raven (Harper & Brothers, 1884). Public domain.
